title: Spa and salon towels with massage oil self-heat in folded stacks overnight after a dryer cycle is cut short before cool-down
problem: Spa, salon, massage-clinic and hotel-spa towels carry treatment oils that low-temperature washes don't remove. Staff open the dryer mid-cycle or skip the cool-down to save time, then fold and stack warm towels. The stack self-heats and ignites after close (LFB Islington spa blaze; Chingford salon fire after towels left in a dryer overnight). A salon/spa fire typically costs ~£20k–£250k+ in damage and weeks of lost trading, and insurers question whether the business followed fire-service advice.
who_suffers: Spa/salon managers, therapists who do the laundry, hotel spa owners
buyer: Owner or Operations Manager of a multi-site salon/spa/hotel-spa group (bought through their laundry-equipment service contract)
industry: On-premises laundries in beauty salons, day spas, hotel spas and massage clinics
current_workaround: Fire-service leaflets and a notice telling staff to wash at 90°C and air towels before folding; nobody checks whether cool-down cycles finish
sensor_concept: CT current clamp on the dryer supply detects 'hot unload' events (heater stops and the cycle is aborted before cool-down) plus a LoRaWAN/LTE-M thermistor tag on the clean-towel shelf or trolley; alerts if stacked laundry exceeds ~45°C after close; monthly 'dryer discipline' report for the insurer
notes: Strong c10 (many fire-service warnings and named incidents) and c8 (clamp plus thermistor); c6 via laundry-equipment service firms (JLA, Forbes, Miele dealers); c7 likely unserved. Risk: c1 needs insured-loss figures.

title: Care-home tumble-dryer lint screens and exhaust ducts clog between cleans, causing laundry-room fires that force resident evacuations
problem: Care-home dryers run 10–14 h a day. Manufacturers require lint screens cleaned every cycle and ducts cleaned regularly, but night staff skip it, and lint-blocked dryers are a recurring cause of care-home laundry fires. A fire means a night evacuation of frail residents, ~£50k–£500k damage and closure to admissions, while the paper lint-cleaning sheet is blank.
who_suffers: Night care assistants/laundry staff, residents, registered manager
buyer: Group Estates/Maintenance Manager of a multi-home care group
industry: Care-home and nursing-home on-site laundries
current_workaround: Paper 'lint filter cleaned' tick-sheet on the laundry wall; an annual duct clean by a contractor if one is booked
sensor_concept: Low-cost differential-pressure (or exhaust-temperature) sensor in the dryer exhaust plus a current clamp; rising back-pressure flags a blocked screen or duct, and a pressure drop after cleaning logs each screen clean automatically; LTE-M alert and per-shift compliance log
notes: Duty with a per-cycle frequency (c2); c6 via laundry-equipment rental/service contracts that already visit care homes; c8 simple; c4 via fire risk assessment and insurer; c1 needs care-home laundry-fire loss figures.

title: Care homes can't evidence that soiled and infected linen reached thermal-disinfection temperature (65°C/10 min or 71°C/3 min)
problem: HTM 01-04 and CQC infection-control expectations require foul and infected linen to be thermally disinfected. Staff pick the wrong programme, overload the machine or use domestic-grade machines, and nobody can prove a cycle reached temperature. Norovirus and C. diff outbreaks close homes to admissions, costing ~£1k+/day in lost fees, and CQC inspectors ask for evidence.
buyer: Registered Manager / Group Head of Quality & Compliance at a care group
industry: Care-home on-premises laundries (washer-extractors)
current_workaround: Trust in the machine programme; occasional thermal validation at service; no per-cycle record
sensor_concept: Clamp-on surface thermistor on the outer tub/drain plus a current clamp on the heater; firmware infers the time above 65/71°C per cycle and flags cycles that fail; LoRaWAN/LTE-M; monthly IPC audit report
notes: c4 strong (named HTM standard, CQC IPC); c2 daily; c6 via laundry-machine rental firms; c8 risk: an indicative rather than validated temperature, so it must be positioned as a screening log.

title: Kitchen extract ducts cleaned on a guessed TR19 interval because nobody records daily hours of use; insurers contest grease-fire claims
problem: BESA TR19 Grease sets duct-cleaning frequency by daily usage (~12-monthly for light, ~6-monthly for moderate, ~3-monthly for heavy use), and many insurers make TR19 compliance a policy condition. Restaurants under-declare usage to save on cleans, then a duct fire (~£100k+ damage and weeks closed) leads the insurer to argue the interval was wrong.
buyer: Operations or Facilities Manager of a multi-site restaurant, pub or hotel group
industry: Commercial kitchens with canopy extract (restaurants, pubs, hotels, care-home kitchens)
current_workaround: Duct-cleaning contractor sets a schedule from a verbal estimate of hours; post-clean certificate; nothing measures real usage
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the extract-fan motor plus a duct thermistor near the canopy; LTE-M logs daily run-hours and heat load, computes the TR19-required interval, alerts when a clean is due or the fan fails, and stores evidence for the insurer
notes: c4 strong (TR19 named in insurer conditions); c6 strong (TR19 duct cleaners already visit and certify); c8 very simple; c7 likely unserved.

title: Independent washroom-service firms empty sanitary bins on fixed 4-weekly rounds: busy sites overflow and complain while quiet sites waste visits
problem: Sanitary and nappy bins are serviced on fixed cycles regardless of fill. Overflowing bins in busy offices, gyms and schools trigger complaints and contract cancellations (~£1k–£5k/yr each), while ~30–50% of visits to quiet sites empty half-full bins. Small washroom firms compete with Initial/PHS on price and service.
buyer: Owner/Operations Director of an independent washroom-services company (bills per service)
industry: Washroom hygiene services (sanitary, nappy, clinical-offensive waste bins)
current_workaround: Fixed-frequency rounds; ad-hoc extra visits after complaints; paper or app service sheets
sensor_concept: Time-of-flight fill sensor in the bin lid plus NB-IoT/LoRaWAN; fill dashboard, route optimisation and proof-of-service log for customer and duty-of-care records
notes: Buyer and channel are the same firm (c5/c6 strong), c2 continuous; c1 is the weak spot (loss is contract churn and wasted visits, not £5k incidents); c7 depends on how far big-firm 'smart washroom' offerings reach independents.

title: Contract cleaners can't prove wet-floor signs were out during mopping, so supermarket and shopping-centre slip claims settle
problem: Slip claims against retailers and their cleaning contractors typically settle at ~£3k–£25k+ each plus legal costs. The defence depends on proving a reasonable cleaning-and-signage system was operating at the time of the fall. Paper cleaning logs are easily challenged, and contractors carry the claim or the excess under indemnity clauses.
who_suffers: Cleaning operatives, site supervisors, claims handlers
buyer: Operations Director / Head of Risk & Insurance at a contract-cleaning company
industry: Contract cleaning of supermarkets, shopping centres, stations and hospitals
current_workaround: Paper cleaning logs on the wall, CCTV requests that often arrive after footage is overwritten, and the insurer settles
sensor_concept: Accelerometer/tilt tag inside A-frame wet-floor signs logs deployed and folded times; BLE zone beacons give location; LoRaWAN/LTE-M uplink; claims-defence report matching signage to the cleaning schedule and incident time
notes: c1 (claim values) and c2 (daily) strong; c4 via Occupiers' Liability Act and cleaning-system case law; c8 trivial; c7 probably unserved; c6 via janitorial distributors (Bunzl etc.) who supply the signs.

title: Restaurant grease traps overfill between fixed pump-outs; water companies recharge sewer-blockage costs and kitchens flood with backed-up waste
problem: Grease traps and grease-removal units are emptied on fixed contractor schedules. Busy weeks overfill them, fats pass to the sewer and blockages follow. Water companies recharge clearance costs (~£1k–£10k+), can prosecute under the Water Industry Act s111, and a backed-up trap can close a kitchen for days.
buyer: Facilities Manager of a multi-site restaurant/takeaway/QSR group
industry: Commercial-kitchen grease-trap servicing
current_workaround: Fixed monthly or quarterly pump-outs by a grease-trap contractor; visual checks by kitchen staff
sensor_concept: Float level switch in the trap outlet chamber (no probe in the grease layer) plus LTE-M; high-level alert before overflow, pump-out events logged as FOG-compliance evidence for the water company
notes: c6 strong (grease-trap contractors visit on contract); c4 via the s111 and FOG enforcement campaigns; c8 simple float. Risk on c7: some grease-monitor products exist abroad.

title: Accessible-toilet emergency pull cords tied up or cut short by cleaners, leaving fallen disabled users unable to raise the alarm
problem: Approved Document M and BS 8300 require the alarm cord to reach the floor. Cleaners routinely loop the cords up out of the way (campaigns such as the 'Red Cord Card'), and people who fall lie undiscovered for long periods. Venues face Equality Act complaints, reputational damage and injury claims.
buyer: Facilities Manager of a shopping centre, station operator or motorway-services group
industry: Accessible toilets and Changing Places facilities in public venues
current_workaround: Occasional manager walk-rounds; awareness cards handed to staff; weekly alarm tests rarely recorded
sensor_concept: Tilt/reed tag on the bottom bangle of the pull cord detects when it is lifted or looped; LoRaWAN uplink; alert to the cleaning supervisor; weekly test log
notes: c10 strong (disability campaigns, press), c8 trivial, c2 daily; weak c1 (little direct £ loss), so this is mainly a compliance and reputational idea.

title: Independent funeral homes' body fridges fail over a weekend with no temperature log, ahead of statutory inspection in England and Scotland
problem: After the Legacy (Hull) scandal and the Fuller Inquiry's call for statutory regulation, councils have run mass inspections of funeral premises, and Scotland already has an Inspector of Funeral Directors and a statutory code. A body-store failure over a bank holiday leaves the deceased deteriorating, viewings cancelled and the family complaining, with goodwill refunds and reputational loss of ~£2k–£10k+ per case; independents have no record to show an inspector.
who_suffers: Funeral directors, bereaved families, mortuary staff
buyer: Owner of an independent funeral home, or Head of Care/Operations at a mid-size funeral group
industry: Independent funeral directors' mortuaries/body stores
current_workaround: Glance at the fridge display when opening up; handwritten temperature sheet if any; refrigeration engineer once a year
sensor_concept: LoRaWAN/LTE-M temperature probe per body store plus a door reed; out-of-hours alert by phone and SMS; daily signed-off log and an inspector-ready monthly report
notes: c4 is rising fast (Fuller Inquiry, Scottish code, council inspections) and c10 strong (national news); c6 via mortuary refrigeration servicers and NAFD/SAIF buying schemes; c7 risk from generic fridge loggers, so the niche report is the differentiator.

title: No record of where each deceased is or how long they spent out of refrigeration (viewing, dressing, embalming): wrong-body and condition complaints
problem: Deceased are moved between body store, preparation room and chapel of rest, sometimes left in a warm chapel overnight. Misidentification or deterioration complaints lead to compensation (~£1k–£10k+), trade-association discipline and press coverage, and inspection regimes now ask for chain-of-custody records.
who_suffers: Funeral arrangers and bearers, bereaved families
buyer: Compliance/Care Standards Manager at a multi-branch funeral group, or the independent owner
industry: Funeral-home care centres and chapels of rest
current_workaround: Paper ID bracelets and a whiteboard; staff memory
sensor_concept: BLE tag fixed to each body tray or coffin (assigned at admission) plus gateways in the body store, prep room and chapel; logs location and cumulative time out of cold, with alerts for any deceased out of refrigeration beyond ~X hours or overnight
notes: Different quantity (location/time) from the fridge idea; c4 rising (codes require care-of-deceased records), c2 daily, c8 BLE simple; c1 needs sourced complaint/compensation figures.

title: Pet crematoria collect from vets' carcass freezers on fixed weekly rounds: some freezers overflow or fail between visits, others are half-empty
problem: Vet practices hold deceased pets in chest freezers until the pet-crematorium van calls. Full or failed freezers mean decomposing animals, upset owners whose individual cremation is compromised, refunds and lost vet accounts (a practice account is worth ~£5k–£30k/yr to the crematorium). Meanwhile fixed rounds waste driver hours on near-empty freezers. Storage and transport fall under the Animal By-Products Regulations.
who_suffers: Vet nurses, crematorium drivers, pet owners
buyer: Operations/Logistics Manager of a pet crematorium group
industry: Pet cremation services collecting from veterinary practices
current_workaround: Fixed weekly or fortnightly rounds; vets phone when full; drivers find failed freezers on arrival
sensor_concept: Time-of-flight fill sensor in the freezer lid plus a temperature probe, LTE-M; crematorium dashboard drives collection routing and alerts on freezer failure; ABPR collection log
notes: c5/c6 strong (the crematorium owns the routes and already visits every site weekly); c2 weekly; c8 simple; c7 likely unserved; c1 rests on account value and route cost.

title: Out-of-hours access to funeral-home mortuaries isn't logged, the gap the Fuller Inquiry exposed
problem: The Fuller Inquiry showed that unrestricted, unlogged mortuary access lets abuse of the deceased go undetected for years. Its funeral-sector phase urges access control and audit. Funeral homes mostly rely on a shared key and an intruder alarm, so they can't say who entered the body store at 2 am. The exposure is criminal, civil-claim and reputational.
buyer: Owner / Group Compliance Manager at funeral directors
industry: Funeral-home mortuaries and care centres
current_workaround: Shared keys, intruder alarm only, CCTV not covering the body store for dignity reasons
sensor_concept: Door reed plus PIR in the body store and a BLE staff fob; logs every entry with identity, alerts on out-of-hours or lone entry; LoRaWAN/LTE-M; audit report for inspection
notes: c4/c10 strong (inquiry recommendations, national news); c8 simple; c1 weak (no clear £ figure) and c7 risk from generic access control.

title: Embalming-room downdraft extraction not running during embalming: formaldehyde exposure with no record between 14-month LEV tests
problem: Embalmers work with formaldehyde-based fluids under a COSHH workplace exposure limit that is under review. LEV must be thoroughly examined every 14 months. Fans are switched off for noise, or filters clog, and nobody knows whether extraction ran during each embalming. HSE enforcement, ill-health claims and failed audits follow.
buyer: Health & Safety Manager of a funeral group, or the owner of an independent home
industry: Funeral-home embalming/preparation rooms
current_workaround: Annual LEV test certificate; trust that staff switch on extraction
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the extraction fan plus a current clamp or reed on the embalming machine; logs that extraction ran whenever the machine ran, alerts if not; LEV test due-date reminders; LoRaWAN
notes: Different buyer from R01-B-01 (factory LEV); c4 named COSHH/LEV duty; c8 simple; c1 weak to moderate.

title: Families keeping a deceased at home on rented cooling plates: the unit is unplugged or fails overnight and the funeral director only finds out at the viewing
problem: Home wakes and home funerals (common in several faith and cultural communities, and growing) use cooling plates or blankets supplied by the funeral director. An unplugged or failed unit overnight causes rapid deterioration, distress and complaints, and the funeral director carries the reputational and refund cost.
buyer: Funeral director (owner) who rents out cooling equipment
industry: Home funerals and home wakes
current_workaround: Daily phone call or visit to the family; instructions sheet
sensor_concept: LTE-M unit with a temperature probe under the plate and power-loss detection; alerts the funeral director if the plate warms or loses power; log of the care period
notes: c8 simple; c5 owner-operator; small niche with weak c1 and c2. Included as a distinct use case.

title: Deceased left overnight in unrefrigerated removal vehicles or private ambulances instead of going straight to the mortuary
problem: Removal contractors and funeral directors on coroner and hospital contracts are meant to take the deceased directly to refrigerated storage. Recent scandals revealed bodies kept in vans and garages. Breaches lose coroner contracts (worth ~£50k+/yr to a funeral home) and cause public outrage.
buyer: Owner/Contract Manager of a funeral director or private-ambulance firm holding coroner removal contracts
industry: Coroner and hospital removal services
current_workaround: Paper removal sheets with handwritten times
sensor_concept: Reed or load sensor on the stretcher lock in the vehicle plus a cabin temperature probe and GPS (LTE-M); alerts if a deceased stays in the vehicle more than ~X hours or overnight; per-removal custody log for the coroner
notes: c4 via coroner contract terms and upcoming regulation; c5 owner holds contract revenue; c8 simple; c7 likely unserved; c2 is daily for busy removal firms.

title: DC isolators and connectors on commercial rooftop solar overheat and start roof fires between annual thermal-imaging inspections
problem: BRE fire investigations found DC isolators and connectors among the leading causes of PV fires, and RISCAuthority RC62 urges periodic thermographic inspection. Warehouse, farm and factory roof PV fires cost ~£100k to several £m, and insurers increasingly attach inspection conditions or exclusions.
buyer: Facilities/Property Manager of a warehouse or farm estate with rooftop PV; or a solar O&M contractor selling to them
industry: Commercial and agricultural rooftop PV (50 kWp–1 MWp)
sector: Renewable energy – solar, wind, battery storage
current_workaround: Annual visual and thermal-imaging inspection (drone or handheld) if the insurer insists; otherwise nothing
sensor_concept: Adhesive thermistor tags on each DC isolator, combiner and connector cluster, read over LoRaWAN to a roof gateway; alert on rise above ambient and cross-string comparison; insurer report
notes: c1 (big losses), c4 (RC62, insurer conditions) and c10 strong; c8 very simple; c6 via PV O&M firms; c7 gap between pricey module-level electronics and annual drones.

title: Orphaned farm wind turbines with dead 2G/3G monitoring modems sit stopped for days and the owner loses Feed-in Tariff income unnoticed
problem: Hundreds of 50–500 kW farm turbines were sold by makers that have since failed or exited. Their SCADA links ran on legacy 2G/3G modems or are simply unsupported. A grid-fault trip or yaw error can leave a turbine stopped for days before anyone looks, losing ~£100–£600/day of generous early FIT income.
buyer: Turbine owner (farm business), or the independent small-wind O&M company that services it
industry: Small and medium onshore wind (FIT-accredited, farm-owned)
sector: Renewable energy – solar, wind, battery storage
current_workaround: Owner looks out of the window or checks the generation meter weekly; O&M visits every 6–12 months
sensor_concept: Optical pulse reader or current clamps on the generation meter output plus LTE-M; compares output with a cheap anemometer or weather API; 'turbine stopped while windy' alert; automated FIT meter-read report
notes: c1 strong (FIT income), c5 owner-operator holds budget, c8 simple, c7 orphaned fleet underserved; c4 weaker (FIT meter reads only).

title: Small-hydro intake screens blind with autumn leaves, stopping generation and breaching eel-screen and flow conditions
problem: Run-of-river hydro intakes must be screened under the Eels Regulations 2009 and abstraction licence conditions. Leaf fall and storms blind screens within hours, cutting generation (~£100–£500/day lost) and risking overtopping or depleted-reach breaches. Owners drive out daily in autumn to rake screens.
buyer: Owner-operator of private small hydro (estates, farms, hydro developers) or their O&M contractor
industry: Small run-of-river hydro (<1 MW) in Scotland, Wales and northern England
sector: Renewable energy – solar, wind, battery storage
current_workaround: Daily or weekly screen-raking visits; some sites have automated rakers (expensive)
sensor_concept: Two low-cost level sensors (ultrasonic above water, or pressure transducers) upstream and downstream of the screen; head-loss alarm via LTE-M; log for EA/NRW/SEPA licence evidence
notes: c2 strong (daily in autumn), c3 strong (raking visits), c4 named regulations; c1 per-site generation loss is modest, needs figures; c8 OK.

title: Non-domestic RHI heat meters stall, drift or miss recalibration, and Ofgem suspends or claws back years of payments
problem: Non-domestic RHI participants (farms, estates, poultry growers, hotels) are paid on quarterly heat-meter readings for up to 20 years. A failed flow sensor, an unrecalibrated meter or a missed reading leads to payments suspended or withheld after audit. Annual payments are often ~£10k–£100k+ per site.
buyer: RHI participant (farm/estate/business owner) or their biomass O&M/compliance contractor
industry: Biomass boilers and heat pumps under GB non-domestic RHI
sector: Renewable energy – solar, wind, battery storage
current_workaround: Manual quarterly meter reads, photos sent to Ofgem; faults spotted months later at audit
sensor_concept: Optical/M-Bus heat-meter reader plus clamp-on flow and return thermistors and a boiler current clamp; detects 'boiler running but meter not counting' and drift; LTE-M; auto-compiled quarterly submission and audit pack
notes: c1 strong (large ongoing payments at risk), c4 strong (Ofgem scheme rules, suspensions), c2 quarterly; c6 via biomass service firms; c7 gap between generic M-Bus readers and RHI-specific checking.

title: Anaerobic-digestion plants' digestate lagoons and silage-effluent tanks overtop between checks, causing EA river-pollution prosecutions
problem: Farm and merchant AD plants store digestate in lagoons and tanks and silage liquor in effluent tanks. Freeboard rules (SSAFO, ~750 mm for earth-banked stores) and permit conditions apply. Overtopping and bund failures into watercourses bring EA prosecutions and fines of ~£10k–£500k+ plus clean-up.
who_suffers: AD plant operators, farmers, downstream fisheries
buyer: AD Plant Manager / owner-operator of a farm AD plant
industry: Agricultural and merchant anaerobic-digestion plants
sector: Renewable energy – solar, wind, battery storage
current_workaround: Daily walk-rounds and dipsticks; plant SCADA covers digesters but not remote lagoons and effluent pits
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic level sensor over each lagoon and effluent tank (outside ATEX zones) plus a bund float switch; LTE-M; freeboard alerts and daily SSAFO/permit records
notes: c1 and c4 strong (EA prosecutions in the niche), c2 daily checks; c6 via AD biology/O&M contractors who visit weekly; c8 simple level sensing; c7 lagoon monitoring is a gap in plant SCADA.

title: Battery-storage and solar-farm firewater tanks required by NFCC guidance and planning conditions leak, freeze or are drawn down, and nobody checks at unmanned sites
problem: NFCC guidance for grid-scale BESS sets a water supply of ~1,900 l/min for 2 hours (~228,000 litres), often met by on-site static tanks written into planning conditions. At unmanned rural sites, tanks leak, freeze or get used by contractors. A BESS fire with an empty tank means total loss of £m-scale assets and planning enforcement.
who_suffers: BESS asset owners, fire and rescue services
buyer: Asset Manager / O&M Manager of BESS and solar portfolios
industry: Grid-scale battery storage and co-located solar sites
sector: Renewable energy – solar, wind, battery storage
current_workaround: Visual tank checks on quarterly O&M visits, if at all
sensor_concept: Hydrostatic pressure level sensor plus temperature (freeze) probe in each tank and a valve-position reed; LTE-M; monthly compliance report for the fire service and planning authority
notes: c4 strong (NFCC guidance, planning conditions), c8 simple, c7 likely unserved; c1 depends on a rare fire, so c2 must lean on monthly checks.

title: Copper-cable thieves break into solar-farm combiner boxes and cable runs overnight; insurers raise excesses or decline cover
problem: Ground-mount solar farms have suffered waves of DC-cable theft. Raids cause ~£50k–£500k damage plus weeks of lost generation, and insurers now impose security warranties and big theft excesses. Perimeter CCTV is expensive, prone to false alarms and often defeated.
who_suffers: Solar farm owners and O&M teams
buyer: Asset Manager of a solar portfolio (independent owners and funds), or the O&M contractor
industry: Ground-mount solar farms (5–50 MW)
sector: Renewable energy – solar, wind, battery storage
current_workaround: Remote-monitored CCTV towers, security patrols, SCADA string alarms that arrive after the cable is gone
sensor_concept: Reed switches on combiner-box and inverter-cabinet doors plus accelerometers on cable trays and trench covers; LoRaWAN mesh to an LTE-M gateway; instant alerts to the monitoring centre; insurer evidence log
notes: c1 and c10 strong (theft waves in trade press), c4 insurer warranties; c7 risk from crowded CCTV security; differentiator is cheap, cable-level detection.

title: Infrared and red aviation obstruction lights on mid-size wind turbines and met masts fail unnoticed, breaching planning and CAA/MOD lighting conditions
problem: Many onshore turbines and met masts carry planning conditions requiring MOD infrared or CAA visible obstruction lighting. Failures must be reported and fixed promptly. Lights on smaller single-turbine sites are often unmonitored, and failures are found by a passing pilot or a complaint, risking enforcement and NOTAM failures.
who_suffers: Wind farm owners, low-flying military and air ambulance aircraft
buyer: Asset Manager / owner of independent single-turbine or small wind sites
industry: Onshore wind turbines and met masts with aviation lighting conditions
sector: Renewable energy – solar, wind, battery storage
current_workaround: Visual checks at night by staff or the O&M contractor; some lights have basic fault contacts nobody wires up
sensor_concept: Photodiode (visible and IR-sensitive) aimed at each light plus a current clamp on the lighting circuit; LTE-M night-time 'light out' alert and availability log
notes: c4 named conditions, c8 simple, c7 likely gap at small sites; c1 weak (no clear fine data).

title: Bath-water temperature not checked and recorded before every assisted bath: scalding deaths, falsified logs and six- to seven-figure fines
problem: HSE guidance requires care homes to control bath water to ≤44°C and to check it before each bath. Prosecutions follow scalds: Salutem was fined £100k after staff didn't check the water; Aster Healthcare was fined £1.04m for corporate manslaughter, with temperature records found falsified; Greencroft was fined after a resident died of bath burns. Paper bath-temperature logs are routinely blank or invented.
buyer: Registered Manager / Group Director of Quality & Compliance at a care group
industry: Residential and nursing care homes; supported living
current_workaround: Handheld bath thermometer plus a paper bath-temperature chart; annual TMV service
sensor_concept: Waterproof BLE/LoRaWAN dip thermometer that logs a reading tied to room and resident (NFC tap) before each bath, plus a clamp thermistor on the bath hot feed after the TMV that alerts if water above 44°C reaches the outlet; tamper-proof bath log for CQC
notes: c1, c4 and c10 very strong (multiple prosecutions incl. corporate manslaughter), c2 daily, c8 simple; distinct from R01-C-12 (NHS TMV servicing): this is the per-bath check record for care homes.

title: Dynamic air-mattress pumps switched off, unplugged or with alarms silenced: residents develop grade 3–4 pressure ulcers and coroners issue reports
problem: Coroners' Prevention of Future Deaths reports cite pumps switched off (Lawrence), turning systems unplugged (Stannard) and fault alarms turned off while staff only checked for power (Stoke-on-Trent). Avoidable pressure ulcers bring CQC safeguarding referrals, negligence claims of ~£10k–£50k+ and inquests.
buyer: Clinical Lead / Registered Manager at a nursing home, or the mattress rental/service company that supplies it
industry: Nursing homes using alternating-pressure air mattresses
current_workaround: Visual check of the pump display on 2–4-hourly repositioning rounds; paper repositioning charts
sensor_concept: Inline air-pressure sensor on the mattress hose plus mains-power detection; LoRaWAN/LTE-M alert to the nurse's phone or nurse call when pressure is lost or the pump is off with the bed occupied; daily equipment-check log
notes: c1/c4/c10 strong (PFD reports, claims, CQC Reg 12), c2 daily; c6 via rental firms that already visit to deliver and service mattresses; c8 simple; c7 likely unserved.

title: Care-home bedroom window restrictors disengaged or broken between monthly checks: residents with dementia fall from windows and HSE prosecutes
problem: HSE expects restrictors limiting openings to ~100 mm in care settings and has repeatedly prosecuted care-home operators after falls from windows, with fines of ~£100k–£1m+. Restrictors get overridden for ventilation in hot weather or broken, and monthly maintenance checks miss them.
buyer: Group Estates/Maintenance Manager of a care-home group
industry: Residential and nursing homes (upper-floor bedrooms)
current_workaround: Monthly manual window-restrictor check by the maintenance person on a paper or app checklist
sensor_concept: Magnet/reed plus tilt sensor on the sash detects opening beyond ~100 mm or a disengaged restrictor; LoRaWAN; instant alert and automatic monthly compliance report
notes: Different buyer from R01-C-10 (NHS wards): private care groups own the fines (c5 better); c1/c4/c10 strong; c8 trivial; c7 risk from cheap generic window sensors.

title: Medicine trolleys and COSHH cupboards left unlocked and unattended: residents with dementia swallow cleaning chemicals or medicines
problem: CQC inspection reports regularly cite unattended unlocked medicine trolleys and COSHH stores. Residents with dementia have died or been harmed after drinking cleaning fluids or taking others' medicines, leading to prosecutions, civil claims and 'Requires Improvement' ratings that cut occupancy and fees.
buyer: Registered Manager / Group Quality Director
industry: Care homes (dementia units especially)
current_workaround: Policy and spot checks; key on a lanyard
sensor_concept: Reed switch on trolley lid or cupboard door plus a BLE fob on authorised staff; alert if open or unlocked with no fob nearby for more than ~2 min; daily exceptions log
notes: c2 daily, c4 CQC Reg 12/COSHH, c8 simple, c7 unserved; c1 needs sourced prosecution or claim figures.

title: Sluice-room bedpan washer-disinfectors fail to reach 80°C for 1 minute between annual validations, spreading norovirus and C. diff
problem: Bedpan washer-disinfectors must achieve thermal disinfection (A0 60, ~80°C for 1 min, per BS EN ISO 15883-3). Element and thermostat faults go unnoticed between annual services, and outbreaks close homes to admissions for weeks, costing ~£10k–£50k in lost fees.
buyer: Registered Manager / Group Infection Prevention & Control lead
industry: Nursing and residential homes with sluice rooms
current_workaround: Annual service and validation by the manufacturer's engineer; staff trust the cycle light
sensor_concept: Clamp-on chamber or drain thermistor plus a current clamp; per-cycle time-at-temperature calculation, alert on failed cycles; LoRaWAN; monthly IPC report
notes: c4 named standard plus CQC IPC, c2 daily; c6 via sluice-equipment service firms (DDC Dolphin, Haigh, Meiko); c8 indicative only, not validated.

title: Mobility scooters and powerchairs charging overnight in sheltered-housing scooter stores catch fire, forcing evacuation of frail residents
problem: Fire and rescue services warn about mobility-scooter battery fires in sheltered and retirement housing, where residents can't self-evacuate quickly. Fires cause ~£50k–£1m+ damage, waking-watch costs and fire-risk-assessment actions. Managers can't see which scooters charge for 20+ hours or show abnormal heat.
buyer: Head of Retirement Housing / Fire Safety Manager at a housing association or retirement-housing management company
industry: Sheltered, retirement and extra-care housing
current_workaround: Charging-room rules, weekly scheme-manager walk-rounds, fire risk assessments
sensor_concept: Current clamps on designated charging sockets (duration and abnormal current) plus a heat sensor and door contact in the scooter store; LTE-M alerts and an FRA evidence log
notes: Different buyer from R01-B-18 (e-bike hubs); c1/c4 (Fire Safety Order FRA) and c10 strong; c8 simple; c7 unserved.

title: Mobile and ceiling hoist batteries left flat, so staff lift residents manually: back injuries, HSE manual-handling enforcement and resident falls
problem: Care homes depend on battery hoists. Flat batteries (chargers unplugged, old batteries) lead staff to lift manually, causing staff injury claims (~£5k–£50k), resident falls and HSE manual-handling action. Hoists also need LOLER thorough examination every 6 months.
buyer: Registered Manager / Group Health & Safety Manager, or the hoist service company as a value-add
industry: Nursing and residential homes with patient hoists
current_workaround: Charging rota on the wall; hoist service company visits 6-monthly for LOLER
sensor_concept: Battery-voltage and charge-state tap plus accelerometer usage counter on each hoist; LoRaWAN; alerts on low charge before shift change; usage and LOLER due-date reports
notes: c6 strong (LOLER servicing firms already visit every 6 months), c4 LOLER/manual-handling duty; c8 simple; differs from R01-C-17 (finding hoists in hospitals).

title: Exposed radiators and pipes above 43°C in residents' rooms after covers are removed or low-surface-temperature units fail: burns and prosecutions
problem: HSE guidance limits accessible surfaces in care settings to ≤43°C. Residents who fall against hot radiators or pipes suffer serious and sometimes fatal burns, followed by HSE prosecutions and claims. Covers are removed by decorators or contractors, and monthly checks don't catch it.
buyer: Group Estates/Maintenance Manager of a care-home group
industry: Care homes and supported living with conventional radiators
current_workaround: Monthly maintenance walk-round checking radiator covers; infrared thermometer spot checks
sensor_concept: Clip-on thermistor on exposed radiator or pipe surfaces plus a cover-present reed; LoRaWAN; alerts above 43°C or when a cover is removed; monthly compliance report
notes: c4 (HSE HSG220 hot-surfaces), c1 prosecutions, c8 very simple, c7 unserved; c2 monthly checks.

title: Care homes must monitor indoor temperatures during heat-health alerts but take sporadic handheld readings, and heat-related deaths and CQC findings follow
problem: The UKHSA Adverse Weather and Health Plan expects care homes to monitor and record indoor temperatures and keep rooms cool during amber/red heat-health alerts. Older buildings overheat above 26–30°C, and excess deaths among residents follow heatwaves. Records are patchy for CQC and coroners.
buyer: Registered Manager / Group Quality Director
industry: Care homes and extra-care housing
current_workaround: Handheld or wall thermometer readings on paper during heatwaves
sensor_concept: LoRaWAN temperature/humidity tags in lounges and bedrooms; workflow linked to UKHSA heat-health alerts with escalation; automatic log for CQC
notes: c4 and c10 good; c8 trivial; but c7 risk (commodity room sensors) and c1 weak, so this is a lower-confidence entry.

title: Reefers at small ports and inland rail terminals left unplugged or tripped after moves, while technicians walk manual 4–8-hourly reefer rounds
problem: Reefer containers are unplugged for every move and must be reconnected promptly. P&I guidance expects checks about every 6 hours, and carriers cap unplugged time (e.g. 3 h). A missed plug-in or tripped socket spoils a ~£20k–£150k cargo, and the terminal pays the claim when it can't prove plug-in times. Large terminals buy enterprise systems; small ports and depots rely on clipboards.
who_suffers: Reefer technicians, terminal ops, cargo owners
buyer: Terminal Operations Manager / Reefer Manager at a small port, inland rail terminal or container depot
industry: Small/regional container ports, inland intermodal terminals, reefer depots
current_workaround: Manual reefer rounds with paper or handheld logs of plug and unplug times and set-points
sensor_concept: Clip-on current clamp on each reefer power lead at the socket plus LoRaWAN; detects 'not drawing power' for more than ~X min, auto-logs plug and unplug events with socket ID, alerts the duty technician; claims-defence export
notes: c1 strong (cargo claim values), c2/c3 strong (manual rounds), c4 via contract and P&I guidance; c7 gap below enterprise systems (Identec etc.); c8 simple clamp.

title: Hauliers fined up to ~£10k per stowaway found in unaccompanied ro-ro trailers because they can't prove security checks at every stop
problem: Under the UK Clandestine Entrant Civil Penalty scheme, hauliers face penalties of up to ~£10k per clandestine entrant unless they show an effective security system and documented checks. Unaccompanied trailers sit in port and depot parks for hours, and paper checklists don't convince Border Force.
buyer: Transport Manager / Operations Director of a haulier or trailer operator using ro-ro routes
industry: Unaccompanied ro-ro freight via Channel, North Sea and Irish Sea ports
current_workaround: Paper vehicle-security checklists, padlocks, cords and seals, driver photo checks
sensor_concept: Door, roof and curtain-tensioner tamper sensors (reed plus accelerometer) with a GPS/LTE-M tracker; timestamped seal-integrity log at each stop and in port parks; instant tamper alert; penalty-defence report
notes: c1 and c4 strong (statutory penalty and code of practice), c2 every crossing, c5 the transport manager owns the fine; distinct from R01-A-01 (cargo theft). c7 risk from some trailer-security products.

title: Small harbours' lit buoys and beacons fail or drag off station unnoticed, but local lighthouse authorities must report availability to Trinity House
problem: Harbour authorities are local lighthouse authorities under the Port Marine Safety Code and must maintain aids to navigation to availability targets, reporting failures promptly. Small harbours check lights by boat, so a failed light or a buoy dragged off station after a storm can go unseen for days, risking groundings, liability and failed Trinity House inspections.
buyer: Harbour Master / Chief Executive of a trust port, private harbour or marina authority
industry: Small and medium trust ports, fishing harbours, marinas with aids-to-navigation duties
current_workaround: Boat or quayside inspections, mariner reports, annual Trinity House inspection
sensor_concept: Photodiode light-on check at night, GPS position and battery voltage on each buoy or beacon; LTE-M or satellite IoT; off-station and light-failure alerts; availability statistics report
notes: c4 strong (PMSC, Trinity House reporting), c2 continuous; c7 risk (lantern makers sell monitoring), but small harbours may be priced out; c1 weak to moderate.

title: Restricted-area gates at small ISPS port facilities left open or propped, found by DfT security inspectors rather than the port
problem: Under the Ship and Port Facility (Security) Regulations, port facilities must control access to restricted zones. Small bulk and timber ports with few staff leave gates open or propped during operations, and DfT inspectors issue enforcement notices, risking ship-security certificates and customer contracts.
who_suffers: Port Facility Security Officers, gate staff
buyer: Port Facility Security Officer (PFSO) / Port Manager at small ISPS-compliant ports and wharves
industry: Small ISPS port facilities (bulk, agribulk, timber, aggregates wharves)
current_workaround: Security patrols on a schedule, paper patrol logs, some CCTV
sensor_concept: Reed contacts on restricted-area gates plus fence-vibration sensors; LoRaWAN; 'gate open more than X min' alerts and an automatic access-control audit log for DfT inspections
notes: c4 strong (statutory PFSO duties, DfT inspections), c5 named statutory role; c8 simple; c1 weak and c7 risk from generic access control.

title: Container self-storage on unmanned rural yards: padlocks cut overnight, customers' goods stolen and the operator's insurance and reviews suffer
problem: Thousands of small container self-storage yards (often farm diversification) are unstaffed. Thieves cut padlocks or angle-grind doors at night, and each raid hits several containers with ~£5k–£30k of combined customer claims, insurer pressure and one-star reviews. Enterprise smart-lock systems are priced for big indoor self-storage chains.
buyer: Owner-operator of a container self-storage yard
industry: Outdoor shipping-container self-storage
current_workaround: Padlocks, CCTV recorded locally and checked after the fact, occasional owner visits
sensor_concept: Magnetic door contact plus accelerometer (grinding and cutting signature) per container; LoRaWAN to an LTE-M gateway; out-of-hours alerts tied to customer access PINs and times; insurer evidence log
notes: c5 owner-operator (strong), c7 gap below enterprise smart-entry; c8 simple; c6 via container suppliers and self-storage insurers; c4 moderate (insurer security conditions).

title: Empty-container depots' high stacks blow over in gales because de-stacking decisions rely on regional forecasts, not wind at stack height
problem: Industry (ICHCA) guidance requires reducing stack heights or lashing when winds exceed set limits. Depots rely on regional forecasts and gut feel. Stack collapses damage dozens of boxes (~£2k–£3k each) and endanger staff and neighbouring sites, several times a year in exposed coastal depots.
who_suffers: Depot operatives, depot managers, neighbouring sites
buyer: Depot Manager / Operations Director of an independent empty-container depot
industry: Empty-container depots and M&R yards near UK container ports
current_workaround: Watching the Met Office forecast; manual de-stacking when a storm is named
sensor_concept: Low-cost ultrasonic anemometer on a top-tier container plus accelerometers on stack-top boxes to detect sway; LoRaWAN; gust alerts against the depot's stacking-height rules; storm log for the insurer
notes: c2 several storms a year, c1 container damage, c8 simple; c7 risk (commodity weather stations); c4 moderate (industry guidance).

title: RDF and SRF bales stacked on the quay awaiting export self-heat and catch fire, while EA fire-prevention plans demand daily stack temperature checks
problem: Environmental permit fire-prevention plans require daily temperature monitoring of a representative sample (~10%) of bales, and RDF industry guidance discourages probing wrapped bales. Port stockpiles awaiting ships can sit for weeks. Fires close berths, trigger EA enforcement and cost ~£100k–£m.
who_suffers: Port bulk-terminal staff, RDF exporters, neighbouring port users
buyer: Operations Manager at a port bulk terminal or the RDF exporter's logistics manager
industry: RDF/SRF and scrap-metal export stockpiles at UK ports
current_workaround: Handheld infrared thermometer rounds and daily paper logs; fixed thermal cameras at larger sites (expensive)
sensor_concept: Surface-contact thermistor tags pinned to bale faces (no probing) across the stack; LoRaWAN; heat map and rise-rate alerts; automatic FPP daily log
notes: c4 strong (EA FPP), c2 daily, c3 manual rounds; c7 gap below thermal-camera systems; c8 simple, though tag recovery at shipment adds handling. Overlaps the waste sector but the buyer is port-side.

title: Ports can't bill ships for fender and quay damage from heavy berthings because nobody knows which vessel hit when
problem: Heavy berthings crack fender panels, shear chains and damage quay edges. Replacing a fender unit costs ~£10k–£100k+. Unless the port can tie the damage to a specific vessel and time, it can't recover the cost from the owner or P&I club, and damage is often found days later on inspection.
buyer: Port Engineer / Harbour Master at a small or medium port
industry: Small and medium commercial ports and ferry terminals
current_workaround: Periodic dive and visual inspections; berthing reports from pilots; costs absorbed
sensor_concept: Accelerometer and tilt sensor on each fender panel or dolphin; LoRaWAN; impact events timestamped and matched to AIS berthing records; claim pack for cost recovery
notes: c1 strong (fender costs, recoverable claims), c2 monthly impacts; c8 simple; c7 gap between enterprise smart-berth systems and small ports (some retrofit sensors exist in NL).

title: Neglected or abandoned vessels sink at their berths in small harbours, leaving the harbour authority with salvage and pollution bills
problem: Ageing fishing boats, workboats and abandoned leisure craft flood through failed bilge pumps or seacocks and sink at berths or moorings. When owners can't be traced, the harbour authority pays salvage and oil clean-up (~£10k–£100k+) and loses berth income.
who_suffers: Harbour masters, other berth holders, local environment
buyer: Harbour Master / Harbour Manager (trust ports, private harbours, marinas)
industry: Small fishing and commercial harbours, marinas
current_workaround: Daily walk-rounds of pontoons, looking at waterlines, chasing owners
sensor_concept: Bilge float switch plus inclinometer (list) plus battery-voltage tag, fitted to at-risk vessels as a berthing-terms condition; LTE-M; 'rising bilge or listing' alert to the harbour office
notes: c1 strong (salvage costs), c5 harbour owns the loss; c2 moderate; c8 simple; c7 harbour-side (not owner) monitoring is unserved.
